caption_text_source.note: YouTube lists a zh-TW caption track without the ASR flag for both original videos. The published dataset identifies the corresponding .zh-TW.vtt files by source video ID and indexes their timed text. Cue counts in source_videos.json include a few cues absent from the dataset rows. Every cited start time was found in metadata.csv.

topic_alignment.paraphrase: Lee asks about parameters after discussing updates to the harness. At 2333.564 seconds he cites gradient descent, followed by Adam and AdamW at 2336.767 seconds. At 2343.307 seconds he asks whether a machine could design the update algorithm.
Lee recalls the end of the first lecture and explicitly gives 52:17 at 2352.616 seconds.
Lee names PostTrainBench. A language model receives the training target and writes code to train the other model. He describes the training-code output at 2374.505 seconds.
Lee introduces AutoResearch as another example of a language model deciding how to update the parameters of another model.

Lee turns to update algorithms generated by a language model, then asks at 2411.709 seconds whether one can train a model specifically to improve that ability. This is the nearest spoken discussion of the question on PDF p.45. Neither AlphaEvolve nor ShinkaEvolve is named in this passage. At 2422.82 seconds Lee names SEAL, the subject of PDF p.46.
topic_alignment.storyboard_observation: The 2400 s frame still shows the autoresearch chart. At 2410 s the video already shows the SEAL diagram from the following PDF page. These ten-second samples do not show the p.45 panel.

topic_alignment.paraphrase: Part II p.42 links directly to 3137 seconds, inside this cue. The speaker introduces the remaining difficulty of continuing self-improvement, then describes using a strong AI to train a weaker AI at 3141.705 seconds. A stronger agent can perform the three steps to improve the initial student.

The speaker begins the detailed PostTrainBench example. The next storyboard at 3180 seconds displays the task instructions, and at 3215.345–3220.850 seconds the speaker specifies one H100 and a ten-hour budget.

topic_alignment.paraphrase: The official course outline places the gradient descent chapter at 26:17. In that discussion the instructor describes choosing a steep downhill direction at the current location, taking a step, and recomputing the direction at the next location. The linked time begins the chapter and does not mark the precise sentence.

notes: The chapter links to the beginning of each relevant spoken topic rounded down to a whole second. The exception is the explicit reference to 52:17 on the Part II slide, which is retained as printed.

The official YouTube player advertises 320×180 native storyboard frames at ten-second intervals. The relevant frames from both lectures were inspected alongside the distributed NTU PDF; the recording and downloadable slides differ in some headings and in the presentation of the p.45–46 material.

Linked research projects and results reported in the chapter were taken from their authors’ papers or repositories. The recording does not discuss the quantitative CS229, AlphaEvolve or ShinkaEvolve examples published in the chapter.
